title: Problems on Trains
tagline: Year 2 — Crossing poles, platforms, people and other trains

introduction.overview: In train problems the length of the train cannot be ignored. To cross a pole or a person, a train covers its own length. To cross a platform or a bridge, it covers its own length plus the length of the platform. To cross another train, it covers the sum of the two lengths. The distance in every case is divided by the relevant (relative) speed.
introduction.placementRelevance: Train problems are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with unit conversion and relative speed. They are a standard application of time, speed and distance.
introduction.realWorldContext: Scheduling trains on parallel tracks, safe passing distances and timing a train through a tunnel use these calculations.

learningObjectives: Identify the distance covered when a train crosses a pole, platform or another train
Use relative speed for two trains in the same and opposite directions
Find the length of a train or a platform from two crossing times
Handle people walking beside the train

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: km/h × 5/18 = m/s. Distance = speed × time. Relative speed: sum for opposite, difference for same direction.

coreDefinitions: Crossing a pole or a man: distance = length of the train.
Crossing a platform or a bridge: distance = length of train + length of platform.
Crossing another train: distance = sum of the two lengths.
Relative speed: S₁ + S₂ (opposite) or |S₁ − S₂| (same direction).
Speed of a person walking is subtracted or added to the train's speed depending on the direction.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A train is a long object, so "crossing" means that the whole train has moved past a point or object. The distance is the length of the train plus the length of whatever it passes, and the time is distance divided by the speed relative to that object.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write "distance = ?" first. For a pole it is L. For a platform it is L + P. For a train it is L₁ + L₂. Then convert the speed to m/s and divide.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Crossing a pole
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: L in metres, S in m/s.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Length from two timings
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Speed = (P₂ − P₁) ÷ (T₂ − T₁);  L = S T₁ − P₁

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Person walking
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Subtract if same direction, add if opposite.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: A man walking beside the track.

mainNarrative: Convert speeds to m/s when lengths are in metres. A train at 54 km/h moves at 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s. A 150 m train crosses a pole in 150 ÷ 15 = 10 seconds.
For a platform or bridge the distance is the train plus the platform. A 200 m train at 20 m/s crossing a 300 m platform covers 500 m and takes 25 seconds.

For two trains in opposite directions use the sum of speeds. Trains of 120 m and 90 m at 72 and 54 km/h pass in (120 + 90) ÷ [(72 + 54) × 5/18] = 210 ÷ 35 = 6 seconds. In the same direction use the difference: 250 m at 5 m/s takes 50 seconds.

If the train crosses a pole in t₁ seconds and a platform of length P in t₂ seconds, then L/t₁ = (L + P)/t₂. A train crossing a pole in 18 s and a 90 m platform in 27 s has L/18 = (L + 90)/27, giving L = 180 m.

For a man walking beside the track, the train's speed relative to the man is the difference if both move the same way, and the sum if opposite. A 100 m train passes a man running at 6 km/h in the opposite direction in 6 s: the relative speed is 100/6 m/s = 60 km/h, so the train goes at 54 km/h.

deepDiveAspects.title: Both crossings use the same speed
deepDiveAspects.content: The speed of the train is the same when passing a pole and a platform. Equate the two speeds to find the unknown length.

deepDiveAspects.title: Equal-length trains
deepDiveAspects.content: If two trains of equal length cross each other in time t moving oppositely, the relative speed is 2L/t. If their speeds are equal, each is L/t.

solvedExamples.title: Crossing a platform
solvedExamples.question: A 200 m long train running at 72 km/h crosses a platform 300 m long. How long does it take?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The whole train must clear the end of the platform.

solvedExamples.title: Two trains in opposite directions
solvedExamples.question: Two trains of lengths 120 m and 90 m run at 72 km/h and 54 km/h on parallel tracks in opposite directions. How long do they take to cross each other?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The two trains must pass completely.

solvedExamples.title: Length from two timings
solvedExamples.question: A train takes 18 seconds to cross a pole and 27 seconds to cross a platform 90 m long. Find the length of the train.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The extra 9 seconds cover the 90 m platform, so speed = 10 m/s.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Not adding the platform to the distance.

shortcutMethods.title: Distance first

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Use different formulas for every case.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Write the distance (L, L + P, L₁ + L₂) and the relative speed in m/s, then divide.

rulesForApplication: Pole: L. Platform: L + P. Train: L₁ + L₂.
Same speed in both crossings of one train.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Add the length of the train.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing the person and train directions

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Time for crossing a platform must exceed the time for a pole.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Always convert speed to m/s first.

intermediate.explanation: Relative speed = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. Time = 250 ÷ 5 = 50 s.

intermediate.question: A 300 m train crosses a pole in 18 seconds. It crosses a platform in 36 seconds. The platform length is
intermediate.explanation: Speed = 300/18 = 50/3 m/s. In 36 s it covers 600 m, so the platform = 600 − 300 = 300 m.

advanced.explanation: Relative speed = 36 km/h = 10 m/s. Time = 300 ÷ 10 = 30 s.
